# Deterministic Finite Automata (DFAs)

This chapter discusses strategies for understanding and working with deterministic finite automata (DFAs). We will cover the basics of DFAs, including their definition, how to construct them, and how to use them to recognize languages. The approach you find here is unique, but it is designed to help you understand the material in a way that is intuitive and practical, especially for programmers. We will be using a lot of examples and exercises to help you practice and solidify your understanding of DFAs. By the end of this chapter, you should have a good grasp of what DFAs are, how they work, and how to use them effectively.

::: {.callout-important}
## Learning Objectives
- Definition of Determinism, Strings, and Languages
- Strategies for Understanding and Constructing DFAs
- Using DFAs to Describe Languages
:::

## Alphabets, Strings, and Languages

To start thinking about theory of computation, we define a few useful terms. An ***alphabet*** is a finite set of symbols. For example, the binary alphabet is $\Sigma = \{0,1\}$.  A ***string*** is a finite sequence of symbols from an alphabet. A string is not a set and order matters. Some example strings, using the binary alphabet, are $1011$ and $0101$. These are not unlike a string defined with quotation marks in a programming language like C++. You might write `"1011"` in C++ to represent a string. `"1011"` is a string that contains 4 characters. In this book, we refer to the characters as symbols, although, at times, the symbols have meaning. `'0'` is a symbol, an element of an alphabet, but it may also mean the digit 0. In this book, the ***empty string*** is denoted by a tilde, `~`, and is a string that contains no symbols. We often use empty strings in programming as well. In C++, you might set a string equal to the empty string, denoted by `""`. A ***language*** is a set of strings. The alphabet of the language is the set of symbols that can be used to create the strings in the language. You might have a language that contains all strings of even length. This language contains strings such as `""`, `00`, `11`, `0101`, and so on. The language of all strings of even length over the binary alphabet can be denoted as $L = \{w \mid w$ is a binary string of even length$\}$. This is an example of a language that contains an infinite number of strings. We will be working with languages that contain both finite and infinite numbers of strings. You can test out your understanding of these definitions with the following exercises.

::: {#exercise-language-definitions .callout-note}
## Alphabets, Strings, and Languages Exercise
- If the alphabet of a language is $\Sigma = \{a, b\}$, give an example of a string that is in the language.
- Give a possible alphabet for a language that contains the strings `dog` and `kid`.
- Give a possible language that contains the strings `dog` and `kid`.
- If the alphabet of a language is $\Sigma = \{a, b, c\}$, how many possible strings could it contain?
:::

As we continue, we will use these terms, alphabet, string, and language, frequently. Our alphabets are finite sets that define the characters that are allowed in our strings. Our strings are like words; they are an ordered list of characters. Our languages are sets of strings and they will often be infinite sets (having an unbounded number of strings).

## Finite Automata (FA)

***Finite automata (FA)*** are a type of computational model. They are called finite because they have a finite number of states. Automata is generally used to denote a machine and thus, in this text, we will often use the two words interchangably. Automata utilize ***states*** as a kind of finite memory. You might say that a FA can be used to determine if an input string is in the language of the machine. States are represented using circles and machines are made up of states with transitions between them. A state with an arrow coming from nowwhere is called a ***start state***. A state with a double circle is an ***accept state***. We treat FA rather non-traditionally in this text. In our machines, there is only one accept state and it is a halt and accept state. If the machine ever enters this state, it halts and accepts the input string as being in the language of the machine. Later in this chapter we'll talk about how to convert a traditional FA into the kind of machine we use in this text.

## Traditional Finite Automata vs Ramsey Finite Automata (RFA)

Unlike the finite automata presented in this book, a traditional finite automata will not have halt states and it does not typically have an end of string transition. In the real world, many FA will operate continuously (imagine a red light or a vending machine that takes coins). A traditional finite automata will not have halt states, but instead will have accept states represented by a circle within a circle (much like our halt and accept state does). Such states are accept states and thus, traditional FA have a set of accept states. When an automata finishes processing an input string, it will accept if it is in an accept state (state with a double circle), otherwise it will reject the input string. The approach presented in this book is beneficial because it operates more closely to how we program software to operate and it is how the state machines we'll look at in the future operate. A language that only needs to look at the first symbol of an input string, could immediately halt and accept or halt and reject based on that symbol. If your need does not include processing the whole string, then we do not bother in the model presented in this book, which we label as a Ramsey Finite Automata (RFA) after the author.

Converting between the formats is not difficult. To turn a traditional FA into an RFA, turn every accept state into a normal state. To each of those states (that were accept states), add an end of string transition from that state to a halt and accept state. Converting from an RFA to a traditional FA is a bit more complicated as we must take special care to end in an accept state which does not halt. For the most part though, you can turn most states that point at halt and accept into accept states. This is not a foolproof conversion, but it is a good starting point. The main point is that the two models are not that different and you can convert between them with a little bit of work. The RFA model is more convenient for our purposes in this book, but it is important to understand the traditional model as well, especially if you want to read other texts on the subject or are getting assistance from someone who is using the traditional model.
